abstract: Cases of phenotypic convergence are common across the tree of life, and often reflect shared ecological pressures. Studying such cases can provide insights into the repeatability of evolution in nature and help uncover the degree to which similar morphological phenotypes tend to also be driven by convergent molecular mechanisms. Here, we investigate the genetic basis of a convergent phenotype in Xiphophorus, a genus of fish known to possess a wide variety of polymorphic pigmentation traits, which have been shown to play important roles in their behavioral and ecological environments. We investigate a melanic spotting polymorphism occurring in the caudal fin that we call "confetti caudal" in X. evelynae. This trait is phenotypically similar to tailspot polymorphisms in two other Xiphophorus species, diverged from X. evelynae by ~6 million generations. We characterize the developmental progression of this trait and use a genome-wide association study paired with analysis of long-read sequencing data to narrow in on a region containing a structural variant that differs between spotted and unspotted fish. Analysis of RNA sequencing data shows that xmrk, a known pigmentation gene that falls within this region, is differentially expressed. Notably, xmrk has been implicated in the development of tailspots in deeply diverged Xiphophorus species. We suggest that xmrk is responsible for confetti caudal in X. evelynae and has been repeatedly co-opted to drive tail patterns across the genus. Despite confetti caudal segregating at high frequency within X. evelynae, we detect a number of individuals in which the spotting pattern progresses into melanoma. Overall, our results highlight convergent involvement of the same gene in tailspot traits in two distantly related lineages. However, we also find that patterns of association between the tailspot pattern, xmrk, and melanoma vary between species, highlighting the complexity of convergent evolution at the molecular level, with implications for how convergent traits emerge and evolve.
